Perfect & Good Weather Days per Year: World Cities (summary version)

Heads up: this page is showing summary numbers from Nov 23, 2026. The full day-by-day weather data isn't loaded into this page yet. Once it's added (with “perfect” vs. “good” days, 32 tourist destinations, and sliders to change the rules yourself), this notice disappears and the page updates automatically.
Perfect day: high 64–82°F, no rain, mostly clear all day (avg cloud cover ≤35%). Good day: high 64–82°F and a pleasant afternoon (noon–5pm: no rain, cloud ≤50%), so morning fog or an early shower is OK. Good days are filled in for 48 cities so far; the rest arrive Nov 24.

Data & sources (so anyone can check the numbers)
  • Weather: daily records for 2023–2024 from Open-Meteo's historical weather API (ECMWF reanalysis). Temperatures use the era5 model and rain/clouds use the era5 model, chosen automatically as the ones closest to official 1991–2020 station records at 11 test cities (average monthly-high error 1.79°F vs 1.94°F; rain-day error 41 vs 43 days/yr). Each row's Raw data link opens that city's exact daily records.
  • How accurate is the weather data? Both models were checked against official 1991–2020 station averages (temperature error = average miss on monthly highs, 2021–2024). Temperatures are usually within 1–4°F. Rain is the weakest part: the models report more rainy days than stations do, especially in foggy or drizzly places (Lima, Cape Town, Mexico City), so the Rain column is approximate. Known weak spot: ERA5 runs about 4–7°F too warm in summer for coastal California (San Diego, Los Angeles, the Bay Area), because each grid square mixes the cool coast with the hot inland, so those cities show more “too hot” days than locals would feel.

  • Crime index: Numbeo Crime Index (resident surveys of how safe a city feels, not police records). “–” means the city isn't covered.
  • Murder rate: for US cities, the city's 2024 rate from FBI data (via Wikipedia's FBI table), labeled “city”. Violent and property crime rates per 100,000 come from the same 2024 FBI table and exist only for US cities. Everywhere else no comparable city data exists, so it shows the whole country's rate, labeled “country”, latest year, from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime via Our World in Data. Hover a cell for its year. No internationally comparable property-crime data exists, so it isn't shown.
  • Salary: average monthly take-home pay in US dollars from Numbeo (crowd-sourced). Palo Alto/Mountain View uses the average of Numbeo's two city pages, which have few entries. Cities marked “country” have no city figure, so they show the whole country's average income per person (World Bank GNI per capita, Atlas method) divided by 12. That is a rougher number: it is before tax and averages over everyone, including children.
  • Air pollution: 2024 average PM2.5 from the CAMS model via Open-Meteo. Ski resorts: OpenSkiMap. Ocean: Natural Earth coastline. Population: city proper from GeoNames; metro population is the urban-area estimate from Natural Earth (small towns show their region's metro, e.g. Walnut Creek → San Francisco Bay Area).
  • Download everything: cities.csv has every number on this page for every city, plus its raw-data link.
How to read this

Good days checks every real day in 2023–2024: the day's high must be 64–82°F, rain under 0.04 inches, and average cloud cover 35% or less. Each day lands in exactly one bucket, checked in this order: too cool, too hot, rain, cloudy, good.

Winter high / Summer high are the average daytime highs of the coolest and hottest months. Night lows are ignored for the score: a 50°F night does not ruin a 72°F afternoon. Freezing nights shows how many nights drop to 32°F or below.

Air pollution is the 2024 average of fine particles (PM2.5) from the CAMS model: the WHO guideline is 5, US standard 9, over 35 is very polluted. Models tend to read higher than city monitors. Ocean is the approximate distance to the sea coast (±10 miles; bays count, lakes and rivers don't). Ski resort is the nearest operating downhill resort with at least 5 km of runs and 250 m (820 ft) of vertical, from OpenSkiMap; indoor slopes are excluded.

Data comes from a weather model on a grid, not single weather stations, so coastal cities can read a few degrees off. One year (2024) is a short sample. Population is the city itself (GeoNames), not the metro area.
